topicName: Query Translation, Compiled Queries, and Performance Tuning
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Query Translation, Compiled Queries, and Performance Tuning in .NET"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Entity Framework Core (EF Core) translates LINQ queries into database-specific SQL. Understanding how query translation works, leveraging compiled queries for repeated execution, and applying targeted performance tuning are critical for building scalable .NET applications."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding EF Core Query Translation"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you write a LINQ query in C#, EF Core evaluates the expression tree and translates it into SQL. However, not all C# constructs can be translated into SQL statements. When a portion of a query cannot be translated, EF Core falls back to client evaluation, which can cause severe performance degradation by fetching unnecessary data into memory."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Server Evaluation: Operations like Where, Select, and OrderBy are translated directly to SQL and executed on the database server."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Client Evaluation Warnings: In modern EF Core versions, un-translatable queries will throw an exception rather than silently falling back to client evaluation, forcing developers to fix the query."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Using Compiled Queries for High-Performance Scenarios"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"By default, EF Core caches the translation of LINQ queries so that subsequent executions reuse the translated SQL. However, compiling a LINQ query introduces a small CPU overhead on the first execution. For hot-path queries executed thousands of times, you can bypass this overhead completely by using EF.CompileQuery."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"private static readonly Func<BloggingContext, int, Task<Blog>> _compiledQuery =
    EF.CompileAsyncQuery((BloggingContext context, int blogId) =>
        context.Blogs.FirstOrDefault(b => b.Id == blogId));

// Usage inside your service
var blog = await _compiledQuery(dbContext, 5);"},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Performance Tuning Best Practices"},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use AsNoTracking() for read-only queries to avoid the overhead of the change tracker."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Project only necessary columns using Select instead of fetching full entity graphs."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Avoid Cartesian explosion when using Include() for multiple collection navigation properties by using split queries via AsSplitQuery()."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"var blogs = await context.Blogs
    .AsNoTracking()
    .AsSplitQuery()
    .Include(b => b.Posts)
    .Where(b => b.IsActive)
    .ToListAsync();"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"By mastering query translation mechanics and utilizing compiled queries along with tuning strategies like split queries and tracking behavior, you can ensure optimal database interaction in your .NET applications."}]
